Chapter 5: The Roots of Religious Violence
When you look back at what happened in Utah, it might feel natural to see it as just a tragic, isolated event—a heartbreaking exception in a peaceful place. But the truth? It’s a lot more complex than that.
If you dig into the history of Mormonism, like so many other religions, you find chapters filled with conflict and moments where violence shaped the story. From the very beginning, this faith has tried to walk a difficult line—between following powerful revelations, and dealing with the harsh realities of a world that often felt hostile.
Now, think about the 19th century—those early Mormon pioneers faced wave after wave of persecution. They were pushed from their homes, chased by mobs, and sometimes, the only way to survive was to fight back. These memories of struggle didn’t just fade away; they became woven into the church’s identity, influencing how members saw themselves and the world around them.
Violence, in this setting, wasn’t always just about self-defense. Sometimes, it was seen as a way to keep the community pure. Take the doctrine of “blood atonement”—the idea that some sins were so severe, only the shedding of blood could bring forgiveness. Sure, the mainstream church eventually stepped away from those beliefs, but you know how it goes... old ideas can linger, living on in the corners of people’s minds.
The Lafferty brothers weren’t the first to think that God might demand violence. Throughout history, people have used religious passion to justify actions that, under any other circumstance, would be unthinkable. That’s the thing about faith—it can inspire incredible kindness and courage, but if it’s twisted, it can turn into something dangerous.
Most of us, when faced with religious violence, want to turn away. It’s so much easier to believe these acts are just the work of madmen, not really connected to the faith that also brings so much good into the world. But here’s something worth paying attention to—the truth is messier. The very beliefs that give life its deepest meaning can, in certain moments, become an excuse for cruelty.
After the murders in Utah, the community couldn’t avoid these hard questions anymore. The Lafferty story wasn’t just about personal madness—it was about a culture that sometimes overlooks the risks of unchecked belief. For everyone left behind, the challenge became clear: how do you hold onto the best parts of your faith, while protecting yourself—and others—from its darkest sides?
But the story doesn’t have to end in tragedy. After violence, there’s always a chance for healing. People can come together to grieve, to remember, and to rebuild. For the folks in that Utah town, the road ahead was tough. Yet, as they struggled to make sense of what had happened, they found a deeper understanding of both the power—and the danger—of faith.
